images.text: Vanessa: Supposing I had told you that I wanted my shipment delivered on Monday, what would you have done? ... I see ... Yeah ... What if we had decided to contact a new supplier? Yes. I'm serious. Yes, you should talk to your supervisor. What a bunch of shady, unreliable, slack-jawed, good for nothings.

Peter: Wow! Don't hold back V. Tell me how you really feel.
Vanessa: If there hadn't been a family sitting in the area, I would have used some real colorful language.
Peter: When did you get so angry?
Vanessa: It's my suppliers giving me the runaround! While we were catering a wedding, they suddenly showed up demanding payment for something I had already paid.
Peter: That doesn't sound very professional. If only they had this new technology called a computer, they could keep track of such things.
Vanessa: They just aren't conscientious. I think it's time to give them the boot.
Peter: You've fired people when you worked elsewhere?
Vanessa: No. I've fired a few people while working here. I let a bartender go last year.

Peter: What happened there?
Vanessa: As he was working here, he was also stealing money from the register.
Peter: How did you find out?
Vanessa: I noticed some money missing one day and I suspected something was wrong when I saw the look on his face. So, I checked the security camera and there it was in black and white.
Peter: Caught red handed.
Vanessa: Yep. He didn't even deny it. If only he hadn't been so stupid. The restaurant business has a lot of conniving, underhanded, crooked characters in it.
Peter: You're one of the good ones, V.

The Unreal Past: Conditional Words and Expressions
When you talk about the unreal past, you use past tenses to talk about hypothetical situations. You use the Past Perfect tense for unlikely or unreal situations in the past.
The structure of the Past Perfect tense is:
You use it with an If clause to show that it is the unreal past.
If I had known, I would have …
This means you didn't know, but if you did you would have done something different.

You use expressions like If, supposing, if only, what if followed by the Simple Past if you want to introduce a hypothetical situation or an imaginary condition.
Example:
If only they had this new technology called a computer, they could keep track of such things.

You use expressions like if, supposing, if only, what if followed by the Past Perfect to introduce hypothetical situations in the past.
Example:
Supposing I had told you that I wanted my shipment delivered on Monday, what would you have done?
Look at the following examples from the text:
What if we had decided to contract a new supplier?
If there hadn't been a family sitting in the area, I would have used some real colorful language.
If only they had a better system, they could track orders better.
If only he hadn't been so silly.
You use time clauses to link different clauses and events. Usually, a time clause introduces a subordinate clause in relation to another event found in the main clause.
You use words like as, while or when to talk about simultaneous actions or to talk about a longer background action taking place when something else happens.

You use while to talk about two longer actions happening at the same time.
Example:
While he was working, he was stealing money from the register.

You use as when you want to say that something changes at the same time as another event starts.
Example:
As I was going through the receipts, I realized something was wrong.

You use when to talk about things that happened at a particular time in the past.
Example:
I suspected something was wrong when I saw the look on his face.
While we were catering a wedding, they suddenly showed up demanding payment for something I had already paid.
